text.p: Michael Johnson earned half a million dollars despite failing to finish while Haile Gebrselassie broke a world record but did not earn a cent in a bizarre weekend of track and field.
Two duels, promoted with all the subtlety of heavyweight boxing contests, reached unsatisfactory conclusions in the Dutch town of Hengelo and the Canadian city of Toronto.
If this is truly the future of athletics, struggling to retain its place in an increasingly competitive marketplace, then administrators, promoters and agents will have to think again.
Gebrselassie's two-mile clash with Noureddine Morceli fizzled out early when the Algerian dropped out in Hengelo while Johnson did not complete his 150 metres sprint against Donovan Bailey.
Events off the track at an International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) council meeting in Athens probably had more significance for the main sport of the Olympic Games.

Exasperated by the U.S. governing body's failure to resolve three outstanding drugs cases, the IAAF announced it was banning Mary Slaney, Sandra Farmer-Patrick and a third American whose name was not released.

Slaney, a double world champion at the inaugural world championships 14 years ago, has vehemently denied using banned substances and her husband Richard and lawyer Jim Coleman greeted the decision with outrage.
"This is outrageous," Richard Slaney said, accusing the IAAF of acting above the law.
The IAAF said the suspended athletes would not be allowed to compete at the U.S. championships this week, where the team will be selected for the Athens world championships.

The seeds have been sown for another prolonged court battle between aggrieved athletes and the world governing body, following the protracted battles with American Butch Reynolds and German Katrin Krabbe.
On Saturday, it quickly became apparent that world and Olympic 1,500 metres champion Morceli was in no sort of shape to challenge Gebrselassie over two miles.
The world and Olympic 1,500 metres champion dropped out early, leaving Gebrselassie to race against the clock in a ultimately doomed bid to break eight minutes and pick up a million dollars.
Officially Gebrselassie, who reduced the world record by 2.46 seconds to eight minutes 01.08 seconds, earned nothing for his efforts, apart from honorary citizenship of Hengelo.
"He needed to break eight minutes to earn anything," said his agent Jos Hermens. "But we will speak to the organisers and maybe sort something out."

Gebrselassie's valiant effort to run the equivalent of two sub-four minute miles was essentially no different from any world record attempt, namely designated pacemakers early in the race followed by a solo run against the clock.
But it was never a duel and Morceli's pre-race comments, in which he indicated he was not taking the race seriously, suggest it was never was going to be a genuine contest.
If Saturday was anti-climax, Sunday's 150 metres showdown between Johnson and Bailey bordered on the tasteless.
Canadian Bailey, who broke the world 100 metres record in last year's Atlanta Olympics, appeared genuinely aggrieved that he had not received appropriate recognition in the United States.

He led American Johnson, the Olympic 200 and 400 metres champion, out of the blocks, at the bend and was still accelerating when Johnson grabbed at his left thigh and hobbled to a standstill with 30 metres to run.
"He's just a chicken," said Bailey, richer by one and a half million dollars, in a graceless post-race comment. "Michael knew he was going to get hammered after 30 metres."
Maybe he did. Maybe there will be a rematch. But after Sunday, it is difficult to see that anybody will care.
